巴洛克吉他為有品弦鳴樂器，約一六〇〇至一七五〇年間使用，與西班牙及伊比利亞半島相: The baroque guitar is a fretted chordophone used roughly between 1600 and 1750, associated with Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-5. The instrument has five courses of gut strings, the highest course sometimes a single string, and movable gut frets. Players took the figured bass in the ensembles of the day, improvising chordal accompaniment, and the instrument may also have been used on its own to accompany.
巴洛克吉他的琴身採用歐洲雲杉或意大利松木製作音板，背板與側板則使用玫瑰木、梧桐木: The body of the baroque guitar has a soundboard of European spruce or Italian pine, with back and sides of hardwood such as rosewood, sycamore or maple. The neck is of mahogany or maple, and the fingerboard is designed with movable gut frets. The strings are all of sheep gut, in five courses, the first often a single string. Decoration may use inlay of ivory, ebony or bone. The whole structure is built for resonance and a warm timbre.
巴洛克吉他約1600至1750年間使用，屬弦鳴樂器，有腸弦五組與可移動腸弦品。最: The baroque guitar was used between about 1600 and 1750; it is a chordophone with five courses of gut strings and movable gut frets. The earliest record of a five-string guitar is in the 1555 work of the Spaniard Juan Bermudo; around 1590 Juan Carlos Amat published the first treatise on the baroque guitar. In the ensembles of the day it often took the continuo, the player improvising chordal accompaniment, and it may also have accompanied on its own; it is closely tied to the development of alfabeto notation. Seventeenth-century sources record three tunings, with octave-strung pairs common early on; at the end of the eighteenth century players in southern France and Italy changed to five single strings.
巴洛克吉他約在1600至1750年間用於同時代合奏，主要擔任通奏低音樂器，演奏者: The baroque guitar was used in the ensembles of its time between about 1600 and 1750, mainly as a continuo instrument, the player improvising chordal accompaniment; it may have joined another continuo instrument in supporting the bass line, and in many cases it may also have accompanied on its own. Works from the sources that can be heard include Gaspar Sanz's Instrucción de música sobre la guitarra española, Robert de Visée's Livre de guitare dédié au Roy and Santiago de Murcia's Resumen de acompañar la parte con la guitarra, which show its uses in accompaniment and as guitar music.
巴洛克吉他音色溫潤而柔和，帶有獨特的古樸質感。由於採用腸弦製作，其音色相較現代鋼: The baroque guitar's timbre is warm and soft, with a distinctive old-fashioned quality. Because it is strung in gut, it sounds warmer and more inward than a modern steel-strung guitar rather than bright and edgy. The instrument's range spans two octaves, and the middle and upper register is especially elegant. The five courses give it rich layers of resonance: the bass is full and deep, the treble clear but not sharp. Beside the Renaissance guitar the baroque guitar is louder and fuller in tone; beside the modern classical guitar it sounds more inward and refined. Its resonance is distinctive, and the movable gut frets add to the warmth, so that in baroque music it produces an elegant and expressive effect, particularly suited to accompaniment and chamber playing.
